title: Given a Scenario, Modify Enterprise Capabilities to Enhance Security

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Organizations often already own the security capability they need, but the control must be configured correctly to reduce the identified risk.
Objective 4.5 asks you to recognize which enterprise capability should change and which modification most directly addresses the scenario.
Use this decision pattern: identify the problem, identify the existing control, and change the setting that produces the required protection.

entries.title: Enterprise Capability Decision
paragraphs: Enterprise security improvements may involve firewalls, IDS/IPS, web filters, operating-system controls, secure protocols, DNS and email security, endpoint monitoring, network admission, or data protection.
entries.recognitionCue: Identify the risk first, then modify the control that addresses it most directly.

sections.callout: Ask what capability already exists and what change would make it more effective.

sections.title: Firewall Controls
paragraphs: A firewall permits or blocks network traffic according to policy. Effective changes narrow access to only the communications the organization actually requires.

entries.title: Firewall
paragraphs: A firewall enforces traffic policy between networks, hosts, or trust zones.
entries.recognitionCue: Permit or block network traffic according to policy -> Firewall

entries.title: Rules
paragraphs: A firewall rule is an individual instruction that evaluates conditions such as source, destination, direction, port, or protocol and then permits or denies matching traffic.
entries.recognitionCue: Individual traffic condition and action -> Firewall rule

entries.title: Access Lists
paragraphs: An access list is a collection of permit and deny entries used by firewalls, routers, and other network devices to filter communications.
entries.recognitionCue: Collection of permit/deny entries -> Access list

entries.title: Ports/Protocols
paragraphs: Port and protocol restrictions harden a firewall by allowing only required services and blocking unnecessary communication methods.
entries.memoryHook: If the business does not need the service, do not leave the door open.
entries.recognitionCue: Restrict unnecessary transport endpoints and protocols -> Firewall hardening

entries.title: Screened Subnets
paragraphs: A screened subnet places public-facing services in a separate network between less-trusted networks and the protected internal environment.
entries.recognitionCue: Separate public-facing systems from internal systems -> Screened subnet

table.caption: Firewall configuration concepts
rows: Isolate public-facing systems from the internal network

sections.title: IDS/IPS Trends and Signatures
paragraphs: An intrusion detection system identifies suspicious activity, while an intrusion prevention system can also block or prevent the detected activity.

entries.title: IDS/IPS
paragraphs: IDS/IPS technology examines activity for attacks. Detection alerts; prevention can act inline to stop matching traffic.
entries.recognitionCue: Detect attacks, with prevention capable of blocking them -> IDS/IPS

entries.title: Trends
paragraphs: Trend-based detection identifies suspicious patterns or changes that develop over time, such as growing authentication failures or unusual traffic volume.
entries.recognitionCue: Suspicious pattern developing over time -> Trend

entries.title: Signatures
paragraphs: A signature represents a known malicious fingerprint that observed activity can be compared against.
entries.recognitionCue: Known attack pattern or fingerprint -> Signature

table.caption: Trend and signature detection
rows: Behavior changes or develops over time
Activity matches a known malicious pattern

sections.title: Web Filtering
paragraphs: A web filter governs access to websites and web content. The best implementation depends on where filtering must occur and what evidence the policy uses.

entries.title: Web Filter
paragraphs: A web filter allows, inspects, or blocks web destinations and content according to organizational policy.
entries.recognitionCue: Control access to websites and web content -> Web filter

sections.title: Agent-Based Filtering and Centralized Proxies
paragraphs: The deployment clue determines whether policy follows the device or traffic passes through a shared checkpoint.

entries.title: Agent-Based
paragraphs: Agent-based filtering installs software on the endpoint, allowing policy enforcement even when the device is away from the organization's local network.
entries.recognitionCue: Web filtering software installed on the endpoint -> Agent-based

entries.title: Centralized Proxy
paragraphs: A centralized proxy receives web requests for users and applies inspection, logging, and policy at one controlled point.
entries.recognitionCue: Central intermediary inspects users' web requests -> Centralized proxy

sections.title: Web-Filter Decision Methods
paragraphs: Web filters can judge a request by its address, content type, an explicit policy, or the destination's known history.

entries.title: Universal Resource Locator (URL) Scanning
paragraphs: URL scanning examines a requested web address for indicators of a malicious or prohibited destination.
entries.recognitionCue: Evaluate the requested web address -> URL scanning

entries.title: Content Categorization
paragraphs: Content categorization groups websites by purpose or subject so policy can allow or block categories such as social media, gambling, or malware.
entries.recognitionCue: Classify websites by content type -> Content categorization

entries.title: Block Rules
paragraphs: A block rule explicitly denies a site, domain, content category, or other defined web destination.
entries.recognitionCue: Defined policy says access is denied -> Block rule

entries.title: Reputation
paragraphs: Reputation filtering uses a destination's history or risk score, including associations with malware, phishing, or spam.
entries.recognitionCue: Trustworthiness or known history determines access -> Reputation

sections.title: Operating-System Security
paragraphs: Platform-level controls centrally enforce configuration and access decisions across managed systems.

entries.title: Operating System Security
paragraphs: Operating-system security uses host-level settings and policy mechanisms to enforce secure configuration and access.
entries.recognitionCue: Platform-level control of host configuration and access -> Operating-system security

entries.title: Group Policy
paragraphs: Group Policy centrally configures Windows users and computers, including password policies, security settings, software restrictions, and administrative controls.
entries.recognitionCue: Centralized Windows configuration enforcement -> Group Policy

entries.title: SELinux
paragraphs: Security-Enhanced Linux adds mandatory access-control policy that restricts what users, processes, and services may access.
entries.recognitionCue: Linux mandatory access-control enforcement -> SELinux

sections.title: Implementation of Secure Protocols
paragraphs: Secure communication depends on choosing a protected protocol, permitting the appropriate port, and selecting a transport method that satisfies the requirement.

entries.title: Implementation of Secure Protocols
paragraphs: Implementing secure protocols means configuring protected communication methods rather than relying on insecure alternatives or incomplete network settings.
entries.recognitionCue: Select and configure protected communication methods -> Implementation of secure protocols

entries.title: Protocol Selection
paragraphs: Protocol selection chooses a secure service, such as HTTPS instead of HTTP or SSH instead of Telnet.
entries.recognitionCue: Choose the communication protocol with the required protection -> Protocol selection

entries.title: Port Selection
paragraphs: Port selection allows the network endpoint required by the approved secure protocol while avoiding unnecessary or insecure services.
entries.recognitionCue: Choose or permit the correct network port -> Port selection

entries.title: Transport Method
paragraphs: The transport method determines how protected communication is carried, including reliability, encryption, tunneling, and TCP-versus-UDP requirements.
entries.recognitionCue: Determine how protected data travels between systems -> Transport method

sections.title: DNS Filtering
paragraphs: DNS filtering stops access earlier in the connection process by refusing to resolve a prohibited or malicious domain name.

entries.title: DNS Filtering
paragraphs: DNS filtering prevents users or systems from obtaining the address of a known malicious or prohibited domain.
entries.memoryHook: Do not give the device the address of the dangerous destination.
entries.recognitionCue: Block a malicious domain during name resolution -> DNS filtering

sections.title: Email Security
paragraphs: Email security combines sender authorization, message signatures, failure-handling policy, reporting, and centralized inspection.

entries.title: Email Security
paragraphs: Email security controls reduce spoofing, phishing, malware delivery, and other message-based threats.
entries.recognitionCue: Authenticate senders and inspect message traffic -> Email security

entries.title: Sender Policy Framework (SPF)
paragraphs: SPF uses a DNS record to identify the mail servers authorized to send messages for a domain.
entries.recognitionCue: Is this server authorized to send for the domain? -> SPF

entries.title: DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM)
paragraphs: DKIM uses a domain-controlled cryptographic signature to help verify that a message was authorized and was not improperly altered in transit.
entries.recognitionCue: Cryptographically verify email origin and integrity -> DKIM

entries.title: Domain-Based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance (DMARC)
paragraphs: DMARC builds on SPF and DKIM alignment, publishes how receivers should handle authentication failures, and supports reporting.
entries.memoryHook: DMARC supplies the policy and reporting.
entries.recognitionCue: Policy for handling email-authentication failures -> DMARC

entries.title: Email Gateway
paragraphs: An email gateway sits between external and internal mail systems to inspect or filter spam, malware, attachments, links, and phishing attempts.
entries.recognitionCue: Central security checkpoint for inbound and outbound email -> Email gateway

table.caption: Email-authentication roles
rows: Is the signed message authentic and intact?
What should happen when authentication checks fail?

sections.title: File Integrity Monitoring and DLP
paragraphs: One control watches whether protected files changed; the other controls whether sensitive information is moving outside approved boundaries.

entries.title: File Integrity Monitoring
paragraphs: File integrity monitoring detects unauthorized or unexpected changes to system, configuration, and application files.
entries.recognitionCue: Detect an unexpected protected-file change -> FIM

entries.title: DLP
paragraphs: Data loss prevention detects or blocks unauthorized use or movement of sensitive information through endpoints, email, cloud services, file transfers, or network traffic.
entries.recognitionCue: Prevent sensitive information from leaving approved boundaries -> DLP

table.caption: FIM and DLP
rows: Is sensitive information leaving or being used improperly?

sections.title: Network Access Control
paragraphs: Network admission can depend on both identity and device health rather than merely physical or wireless connectivity.

entries.title: Network Access Control (NAC)
paragraphs: NAC evaluates a user or device's identity, security posture, and compliance before allowing, restricting, blocking, or quarantining network access.
entries.recognitionCue: Evaluate a user or device before network admission -> NAC

sections.title: EDR and XDR
paragraphs: Detection and response may focus on endpoint telemetry or correlate evidence across several security domains.

entries.title: EDR/XDR
paragraphs: Endpoint Detection and Response continuously monitors endpoint activity for detection, investigation, isolation, and response. Extended Detection and Response correlates evidence across endpoints, email, networks, cloud systems, identities, and other sources.
entries.memoryHook: EDR focuses on endpoints; XDR extends across the environment.
entries.recognitionCue: Endpoint detection and response extended across multiple security sources -> EDR/XDR

sections.title: User Behavior Analytics
paragraphs: Behavior analytics establishes a normal activity pattern and highlights deviations that may require investigation.

entries.title: User Behavior Analytics
paragraphs: UBA identifies unusual user activity such as abnormal access, unexpected geography, large downloads, or logins at unusual times.
entries.recognitionCue: Detect anomalies by comparing activity with expected user patterns -> User behavior analytics

sections.title: Recognition Cues
paragraphs: Permit or deny traffic -> Firewall rule | Collection of permit/deny entries -> Access list | Separate public services -> Screened subnet
Known malicious pattern -> Signature | Suspicious pattern over time -> Trend

Filtering follows the endpoint -> Agent-based | Shared web checkpoint -> Centralized proxy | Inspect address -> URL scanning | Group websites -> Content categorization | Explicit denial -> Block rule | Destination history -> Reputation
Central Windows policy -> Group Policy | Linux mandatory controls -> SELinux | Safer communication technology -> Protocol selection | Block malicious name resolution -> DNS filtering
Authorized mail server -> SPF | Signed email -> DKIM | Failure policy and reporting -> DMARC | Central mail inspection -> Email gateway
Detect file changes -> FIM | Stop sensitive-data movement -> DLP | Check before network admission -> NAC
Endpoint response -> EDR | Cross-platform response -> XDR | Abnormal user activity -> UBA

entries.title: Capability Selection
paragraphs: Name the risk category first: traffic, web access, email, endpoint, data, network admission, or behavior.
entries.recognitionCue: Problem category -> existing capability -> most direct configuration change

sections.title: Objective 4.5 Exam Trap
paragraphs: SPF authorizes sending servers; DKIM verifies a domain signature; DMARC defines policy and reporting for failed alignment.
FIM asks whether a protected file changed; DLP asks whether sensitive information is leaving or being used improperly.
NAC decides whether a user or device should join the network; a firewall decides whether particular traffic should pass.
EDR focuses on endpoints; XDR correlates across a broader set of security domains.
A signature matches a known pattern; a trend identifies behavior developing over time.
DNS filtering blocks name resolution; web filtering evaluates web destinations, requests, or content.
sections.callout: Ask what capability the scenario wants changed: traffic, web access, email, endpoint, data, identity behavior, or network admission.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
paragraphs: Control traffic -> Firewall | Public systems separated -> Screened subnet | Known fingerprint -> Signature | Pattern over time -> Trend
Filter on endpoint -> Agent-based | Filter through one checkpoint -> Proxy | Check URL -> URL scanning | Group site types -> Content categorization | Known bad history -> Reputation
Manage Windows policy -> Group Policy | Restrict Linux processes -> SELinux | Use safer protocol -> Protocol selection | Stop a dangerous DNS lookup -> DNS filtering
Authorized email server -> SPF | Signed message -> DKIM | Authentication policy/reporting -> DMARC | Filter mail centrally -> Email gateway
Watch file changes -> FIM | Stop sensitive-data loss -> DLP | Check network admission -> NAC
Endpoint detection/response -> EDR | Broader detection/response -> XDR | User acting unusually -> UBA

entries.title: Final Decision Cue
paragraphs: Select the control whose configuration change acts closest to the risk described in the scenario.
entries.recognitionCue: Risk -> control -> setting -> reduced exposure

miniCheck.intro: Choose the sender-authorization control and the receiver-policy control.
miniCheck.prompt: A company is reducing forged email that impersonates its domain. It must publish which mail servers are allowed to send on the domain's behalf. It must also tell receiving systems to quarantine messages that fail aligned email-authentication checks and collect reports about those failures.

fields.label: Control that identifies authorized sending servers
choices: Domain-Based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance (DMARC)

fields.label: Control that defines failure handling and reporting
choices: Domain-Based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance (DMARC)
fields.answer: Domain-Based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance (DMARC)

miniCheck.correctFeedback: Correct. SPF publishes which mail servers may send for the domain. DMARC uses SPF and DKIM alignment to define receiver handling for authentication failures and provide reporting.
miniCheck.retryFeedback: Not quite. Choose the control that lists authorized sending servers, then choose the control that publishes failure-handling policy and reporting. Review Email Security and try again.
